analysis.one_liner: Exempts alternative-fuel vehicle conversions and biomass fuels from Clean Air Act oversight and gives automakers a fuel-economy compliance bonus.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee with no cosponsors and no action after its May 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite parts of the Clean Air Act and federal fuel-economy law to make it easier to sell and install alternative-fuel technology. Converting a car to run on propane, natural gas, or similar fuels would no longer need an EPA certification as long as the installer shows good engineering work, and the EPA could not prohibit or control biomass fuel. Automakers whose fleets are at least half made up of vehicles that can run on alternatives to gasoline — ethanol blends, biodiesel, natural gas, hydrogen, propane, or electricity — would get 8 miles per gallon added to their official fuel-economy average and would be automatically counted as meeting Clean Air Act greenhouse gas rules.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be biofuel producers — especially ethanol and biomass fuel makers, who gain guaranteed market access — and automakers, who could meet fuel-economy and greenhouse gas rules more easily by selling alternative-fuel-capable vehicles and collecting an 8-mpg bonus. Aftermarket conversion shops also gain from dropping the EPA certification requirement. Consumers who want non-gasoline fuel options might see more choices and possibly lower fuel prices in markets where ethanol-blend limits currently bind.

how_it_helps.text: Aftermarket conversions of vehicles to run on alternative fuel are exempted from the Clean Air Act's 'tampering' rules and from the EPA certificate-of-conformity requirement, provided the installer shows the conversion is well designed and does not degrade emissions; a label must be affixed and the EPA can still ban a bad system if it has evidence [S2].
The EPA is barred from prohibiting or controlling biomass fuel under the Clean Air Act, giving biomass fuel producers a statutory guarantee they cannot be regulated out of the market [S2].

Manufacturers whose fleets are at least 50 percent 'fuel choice enabling' — able to run on natural gas, hydrogen, propane, 20 percent biodiesel, E85, or electricity — get 8 mpg added to their regulatory fuel-economy average and are deemed in compliance with EPA greenhouse gas rules [S2].

Fuel-economy credits can be carried five model years forward instead of the previous window, and the Clean Air Act's ethanol-blend waiver provisions are loosened to ease sales of gasoline with higher ethanol content [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The cost, if any, falls on public oversight: emissions performance of converted vehicles would be guaranteed mainly by the installer's own judgment rather than an EPA certificate, biomass fuel would be placed beyond the EPA's control, and the automaker bonus could let fleets consume more gasoline while still counting as compliant. Air quality and consumers' exposure to higher fuel use would absorb that risk.

drawbacks.text: An aftermarket conversion no longer needs an EPA certificate of conformity as long as the installer claims good engineering judgment; EPA can only act after it has evidence that a system degrades emissions, shifting enforcement from prevention to after-the-fact policing of vehicles already on the road [S2].
The bill bars the EPA from prohibiting or controlling biomass fuel under the Clean Air Act, removing a regulatory tool for addressing fuel-related emissions no matter what future evidence shows [S2].

Adding 8 mpg to the calculated fuel economy of manufacturers whose fleets are at least half 'fuel choice enabling,' and deeming their vehicles compliant with greenhouse gas rules, could let automakers sell fleets that burn more gasoline while counting as fully compliant [S2].
The amendments would let manufacturers bank fuel-economy credits for five model years beyond the year earned, loosening the pace at which fleet efficiency standards force improvement [S2].
Weakening the Clean Air Act's controls on ethanol blends and conversions could increase smog-forming emissions in vehicles that are not designed to handle them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the industries it targets, the bill is a clear win: fewer EPA certifications, a statutory shield for biomass fuels, and a free 8-mpg compliance bonus for automakers that diversify their fleets. For the public, the honest case is that consumers could get more fuel options and possibly lower fuel costs in some markets. The honest cost is that each gain is paid for with weaker oversight: emissions performance is taken on the manufacturer's word, biomass fuel is placed beyond EPA control by statute, and the CAFE bonus and deemed-compliance provisions could let automakers sell fleets that use more gasoline while staying in compliance. The bill never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be weighed in a hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: Rand Paul introduced it and it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and no one signed on as a cosponsor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 21, 2025 [S1] [S4].
The only recorded action besides introduction was that the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works [S4].

The bill would exempt qualified aftermarket alternative-fuel conversions from Clean Air Act certification and tampering rules, bar the EPA from prohibiting or controlling biomass fuel, and give manufacturers with majority alternative-fuel-capable fleets an 8-mpg fuel-economy bonus and deemed compliance with greenhouse gas rules [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed: existing EPA oversight of fuel conversions and biomass fuels, and the current fuel-economy compliance rules, remain in place. No industry gained anything yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; existing fuel rules remain

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a hearing, vote, or cosponsor, so no one — in either party — was recorded for or against it.

industries.note: The bill makes biomass fuel unregulable under the Clean Air Act and loosens the provisions governing higher ethanol-gasoline blends. Ethanol interests gain guaranteed market access, though some consumer benefit (potentially cheaper blends) travels with them.

A statutory 8-mpg bonus on their fuel-economy average, deemed compliance with EPA greenhouse gas rules, and a longer credit-carry window let automakers meet federal standards with less actual fuel-economy improvement. The public cost is potentially higher fleet gasoline consumption.

Conversions to alternative fuel no longer require EPA certification and cannot be treated as tampering if the installer attests to good engineering. Enforcement shifts from prevention to after-the-fact orders only when the EPA already has evidence of harm.

industries.industry: Propane, natural gas, and hydrogen fuel suppliers
industries.note: The bill defines and rewards manufacturers selling vehicles that run on these fuels, expanding their potential vehicle market. Consumers gain fuel choice, but without the emissions certification the current law requires.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no hearing, and no committee action more than a year into a two-year Congress, the bill is highly unlikely to move. Single-sponsor deregulation bills at this stage typically sit in committee and expire when the Congress ends in January 2027 unless the sponsor secures committee attention or attaches the provisions to a larger vehicle bill.
